assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, are a clear case of a new instrument that opens a door: fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 turns clocks into probes of gravity, fundamental constants and geodesy, and prepares a redefinition of the second. The invention is concrete and measurable.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstrations; Jun Ye's group brought the clock to the highest accuracy and stability with strontium. Two laureates fit the original-work criterion; Ye's frequency-comb and cold-atom contributions overlap with earlier prizes (2005, 2012), which must be weighed. Other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Hollberg, Lisdat) contributed.
assessment.maturity: Many independent clocks worldwide agree at the 1e-18 level, and intercomparisons are routine. Recognition is timely, with the SI second redefinition under discussion.
uncertainties: Credit for the earliest lattice-clock demonstrations and the break-even accuracy race among strontium, ytterbium and other groups needs checking in the historical record.
Overlap with the 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche) prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Solid-state femtosecond lasers (Ti:sapphire, Kerr-lens mode locking, SESAM) are the enabling instrument for attosecond physics, which the committee recognised in 2023, as well as for ultrafast spectroscopy and frequency combs. The importance and lasting impact are very large, and the work is an invention in the Nobel sense.
assessment.attribution: Moulton introduced Ti:sapphire as a laser medium; Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode locking; Keller invented SESAMs and mode-locked ultrafast solid-state lasers. This fits three distinct and decisive contributions, and a woman would be among the recipients. Contributions by others (e.g. Spence, Sibbett colleagues, Haus on theory) may blur the allocation.
assessment.maturity: The technology has been mature and ubiquitous for decades, so the recognition is, if anything, late. No interpretive doubts remain.
uncertainties: Allocation between Kerr-lens mode locking (Sibbett group versus other co-discoverers) and SESAM work needs checking.
Part of the benefit has already been rewarded via chirped pulse amplification (2018) and attosecond physics (2023).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle opened the field of moire quantum materials, a new tool for controlling electron correlations. The experimental result was unexpected and is clearly an original experiment.
assessment.attribution: Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 experimental observation with the Cao et al. team; Bistritzer and MacDonald supplied the theory that predicted the magic angle. The first author of the experiment (Yuan Cao) is not among the credited names, so a fair configuration needs care. Two or three of the credited names could be proposed.
assessment.maturity: The results have been reproduced by many groups and extended to other moire systems; the field is young but robust. Some physics of the superconductivity is still debated, so the prize would recognise the discovery, not the mechanism.
uncertainties: Mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Allocation between theory and experiment, and the exclusion of junior experimental authors under the three-person limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators combine a theoretical prediction (quantum spin Hall effect, Z2 invariant) with clean experimental verification, first in HgTe quantum wells and later by ARPES in Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3. Their importance for the understanding of matter is high, and they opened a family of topological materials.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the central theory; Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation of the QSH edge states; Hasan's group did the first 3D topological insulator observations. Mele, and Bernevig/Zhang (theory of the HgTe proposal) are part of the history, so the proposed laureates are not uncontested. Credit is also split from the quantum anomalous Hall experiment (not this entry).
assessment.maturity: Experimental verification is strong and independent over more than a decade. Recognition is timely, even somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Mele's role and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal create credit disputes that I cannot resolve from the supplied text.
Priority between competing 3D topological insulator experiments (Hasan versus other ARPES groups).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos by IceCube (2013) and the association with the blazar TXS 0506+056 and with the Galactic plane opened neutrino astronomy and is a large new instrument for seeing the universe. This is an experimental discovery with a clear impact on astrophysics.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube and its predecessors; Karle was a central scientist in the collaboration and in the detector development. Large collaboration credit is difficult, and AMANDA and the Baikal and ANTARES efforts also mattered. I would want the committee to confirm that the two names reflect the decisive leadership.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is established with high significance; source identification is only partial (TXS, NGC 1068). Recognition is plausible but the source picture is still developing.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration attribution and the role of other leaders (e.g. Gaisser, Kowalski) must be checked.
Identification of the sources remains incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nd-Fe-B magnets, the strongest permanent magnets, were discovered in 1982-84 and underpin motors, wind turbines, hard drives and electric vehicles. This is a materials invention with tremendous benefit to humanity and a clear original discovery.
assessment.attribution: Sagawa (Sumitomo) and Croat (General Motors) independently discovered Nd2Fe14B with different processing routes; both are cleanly credited and no more are needed. The independence of the two discoveries could make a fair split possible, but a priority dispute may arise.
assessment.maturity: The impact is decades long and fully confirmed. The question is whether the committee judges it to be physics rather than materials science and engineering.
uncertainties: Whether the discovery is judged to fall within the physics prize.
Priority and credit between the two inventors and associated industrial groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single solid-state colour-centre spins (NV centre in diamond) allow optical readout and coherent control of single spins at room temperature, enabling nanoscale sensing and quantum networks. This is a new tool that lets us see magnetic fields and temperature at the nanoscale, close to my own interests in measurement.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group did the first optical detection of single NV spins (1997); Awschalom's group did extensive coherent control and spin-qubit work; others (Lukin, Walsworth, Hanson, Jelezko) were important for sensing and entanglement. A three-person limit makes the allocation unclear.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories, but the field is a wide set of applications with different pioneers, so a clean prize statement is not obvious.
uncertainties: Allocation among the many groups (Jelezko, Hanson, Lukin, Walsworth, Awschalom, Wrachtrup).
Whether the decisive discovery is the single-spin detection or the later quantum-sensing applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus sensor and CO-functionalised tips gave atomic and bond-resolved imaging of single molecules by force microscopy, an instrument that makes chemical structure visible. This matches my interest in methods that let us see matter atom by atom, though the long-term impact is more limited than for the entries above.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor and its use at small amplitude; Gross, Meyer and colleagues at IBM Zurich demonstrated the molecular bond imaging in 2009. The invention and the later demonstration are different steps and the original atomic force microscopy (Binnig, Quate and Gerber) is already recognised, so credit is fairly clear but the incremental nature must be weighed.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced worldwide, and the technique is mature. The question is whether the scientific significance rises to the level of a prize in physics or is mainly a chemistry and surface-science tool.
uncertainties: Whether the advance counts as the original experiment or as an improvement on atomic force microscopy.
I have a professional closeness to microscopy that I should be careful about; I cannot independently verify the details of the credit chain.
